title: Korean Soy Garlic Chicken
subtitle: Crispy fried chicken glazed in sweet soy and garlic sauce
excerpt: Boneless chicken pieces are coated in a light flour and egg batter and fried until crisp, then tossed in a sticky sweet soy and garlic glaze that lacquers each piece. This recipe serves 4 and takes around 45 minutes. The double-fry technique used in Korean fried chicken gives it a crunch that holds even after the sauce is applied.
sourceNotes: Korean fried chicken rose to international prominence in the 1970s after American-style fried chicken was introduced to Korea and local cooks began developing their own approach. The double-frying technique produces a thinner, crispier crust than single-fry methods, and the sweet soy glaze is a distinctly Korean development. Soy garlic is now one of the two canonical Korean fried chicken flavours alongside the spicy gochujang version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made up to 3 days ahead and kept in the fridge. Fry and sauce the chicken just before serving.
recipe.temperatureNote: Oil temperature for frying. Use a thermometer if available. Without one, a small piece of batter should sizzle immediately on contact.

glossaryTerms.definition: Korean fried chicken differs from Western fried chicken primarily in the frying technique and the coating. Korean-style chicken is typically fried twice: once at a lower temperature to cook the meat through, then again at a higher temperature to blister and crisp the thin batter. This produces a much lighter, crunchier coating that stays crisp for longer than a single-fry method. The batter is thinner and less bready than American Southern-style fried chicken.

Yangnyeom means seasoned sauce in Korean, and in the context of fried chicken it refers to the sticky, sweet and savoury coating applied to the fried pieces after cooking. There are two classic yangnyeom styles: the spicy gochujang-based red sauce, and the soy garlic version used in this recipe. The sauce is cooked briefly to concentrate it before the chicken is added and tossed to coat.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes around 45 minutes.
gets its characteristic crunch from the double-fry method, and the soy garlic
sauce is sweet, savoury and deeply garlicky. The first fry cooks the chicken through. The second fry, at a slightly higher temperature, crisps the crust.

Keep the pieces to a uniform size when cutting the chicken so they cook evenly. Cut boneless thighs into roughly 5cm chunks. Do not overcrowd the wok during frying: work in two or three batches. Crowding drops the oil temperature and produces pale, soggy chicken rather than crisp, golden pieces.
Coat the chicken. Place the flour in one bowl and the beaten egg in another. Dip each chicken piece first in the egg, letting the excess drip off, then in the flour. Set the coated pieces on a plate.

Make the sauce. Combine the soy sauce, garlic, sugar, mirin, sesame oil and rice vinegar in a small saucepan. Heat over a medium-low heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the sauce thickens slightly. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a wok to 175C. Fry the chicken in batches for 5 to 6 minutes until lightly golden and just cooked through. Remove and drain on a wire rack or kitchen paper.
Increase the oil temperature to 190C. Return the chicken to the wok in batches and fry for 2 to 3 minutes until deep golden and very crisp. Drain again.
Reheat the sauce gently if needed. Add all the fried chicken to the pan with the sauce and toss quickly to coat each piece evenly. Work fast so the crust does not soften.
Transfer to a serving plate. Scatter over the sesame seeds and spring onions and serve immediately.

items.symptom: Chicken coating is pale and soft rather than golden and crisp
items.cause: The oil was not hot enough, or too many pieces were fried at once
items.fix: Fry in small batches of 5 to 6 pieces at a time. The oil temperature drops when cold chicken goes in. Let it recover between batches. The second fry at higher temperature is what creates the deep golden crunch.

items.symptom: Sauce has become very thick and sticky and is burning in the pan
items.cause: The sauce was left on the heat too long before adding the chicken
items.fix: The sauce should coat a spoon lightly, not be thick like caramel. If it has gone too thick, add a small splash of water and stir. Add the chicken immediately once the sauce is ready.

items.symptom: Coating falls off during the second fry
items.cause: The egg and flour coating was too thin or the pieces were moved too much in the oil
items.fix: Press the flour coating onto each piece firmly before frying. Once in the oil, do not move the pieces for the first 2 minutes until the coating has set. Then turn gently with tongs.

content.text: Korean fried chicken is eaten at dedicated chimaek restaurants in Korea, where it is paired with beer. The word chimaek comes from chi (chicken) and maek (beer in Korean). It is a social, communal, evening dish rather than a daytime meal. Soy garlic is the milder of the two main flavours and appeals to those who want the sweetness and umami without the heat of the spicy version. Both are served in enormous platters and eaten with pickled radish cubes on the side.
